title: Execution
author: Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan
theme: Execution is a discipline in its own right, and getting things done is the leader's most important job rather than a detail to hand off.
summary: Larry Bossidy, a veteran chief executive, and Ram Charan, an adviser to many boards, start from a simple observation. Companies rarely fail because their strategy was foolish. They fail because the strategy was never carried out. The gap between what leaders promise and what organisations deliver is, in their view, the biggest unaddressed problem in business.

They argue that execution is not tactics, and it is not something leaders can delegate. It is a systematic way of exposing reality and acting on it, and it must sit at the heart of a company's strategy, goals and culture. The leader has to be deeply and personally involved.

The book rests on three building blocks. The first is the leader's own behaviour. The authors describe habits such as knowing the people and the business in detail, insisting on realism, setting a few clear priorities, following through relentlessly, rewarding those who deliver, and coaching people to grow. Underneath all of these lies emotional fortitude: the self-awareness and confidence to face hard truths and hear bad news.

The second block is a culture that values results. Changing behaviour requires linking rewards to performance and encouraging candid, robust dialogue in meetings, so that problems surface early instead of being hidden behind polite agreement.
The third block is having the right people in the right jobs, a task the authors say no leader should give away. Choosing and developing leaders shapes everything else.

On top of these foundations sit three core processes: the people process, the strategy process and the operations process. Each must be run rigorously, and, crucially, the three must be tightly linked. A strategy is only realistic if it matches the people available and an operating plan that turns it into budgets, milestones and accountabilities.
The overall message is that disciplined follow-through, not brilliant planning alone, separates successful companies from the rest.
takeaway: Stay personally engaged, face reality, put the right people in key roles, and link people, strategy and operations so plans actually get done.

questions.q: According to the authors, why do most corporate strategies fail?
options: They are not carried out well
questions.why: The book argues that the usual cause of failure is weak execution, not a bad strategy.

questions.q: How do Bossidy and Charan view execution?
options: As a set of tactics for junior managers
As something best outsourced to consultants
As a systematic discipline central to strategy and culture
questions.why: They treat execution as a discipline that must be built into how the whole business works.

questions.q: What role should the leader play in execution?
options: Set the vision and leave details to others
Step in only during a crisis
questions.why: The authors insist execution cannot be delegated and requires the leader's active engagement.

questions.q: Which quality do the authors place beneath all the essential leader behaviours?
questions.why: Self-awareness and inner strength let leaders face hard truths and act on them.

questions.q: Why do the authors stress 'robust dialogue' in an organisation?
options: To bring problems and realities into the open
questions.why: Candid discussion surfaces issues early so they can be dealt with rather than hidden.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three core processes in the book?
questions.why: The core processes are the people, strategy and operations processes.

questions.q: What do the authors say about the three core processes?
options: They must be tightly linked to one another
They should be run by separate, independent teams
Only the strategy process really matters
They should be reviewed once every five years
questions.why: Execution depends on aligning people, strategy and operations rather than treating them in isolation.

questions.q: Which task do the authors say a leader should never delegate?
options: Getting the right people into the right jobs
questions.why: Selecting and developing people shapes all results, so leaders must own it themselves.

questions.q: What does the operations process mainly do?
options: Turn strategy into concrete targets, budgets and accountabilities
questions.why: The operating plan converts strategic direction into specific milestones and responsibilities.

questions.q: How does the book suggest changing an organisation's culture?
options: By issuing a new mission statement
By linking rewards to performance and changing behaviour
questions.why: The authors see culture as changing when behaviour changes, driven by rewards tied to results.
